sentences.text: It is further pleaded by the plaintiff that after believing the representation and assurances made by the defendant to be true, the plaintiff in good faith agreed to invest a sum of Rs. 33,00,000/- for setting up of the said restaurant after which she was to be included as a partner.

The amount of Rs.
33,00,000/- was paid in different installments described in para 5 of the plaint during the period from 13.06.2016 to 06.08.2016 through bank account transfer.

5. It is alleged that after receiving the entire amount of Rs.
33,00,000/- the defendant turned dishonest and failed to rope in the plaintiff as a partner as per previous assurances.
The plaintiff made repeated attempts and requests to the defendant to honor its commitments but the defendant kept on delaying on one pretext or the other.

Consequently, the plaintiff demanded the amount of Rs. 33,00,000/- from the defendant and then instead of paying the entire amount, the defendant paid only a sum of Rs. 10,00,000/- to the plaintiff on 26.04.2017 through bank transfer.
The remaining amount of Rs. 23,00,000/- still remained unpaid.

6. It is further pleaded that on persistent reminders and requests made by the plaintiff for payment of the balance amount of Rs. 23,00,000/-, the defendant issued cheque bearing No. 000181 dated 15.07.2017 for a sum of Rs. 23,00,000/- drawn on Kotak Mahindra Bank, Netaji Subhash Place in discharge of its liability towards the plaintiff.
On presentation, the said cheque was returned unpaid with remark, "Insufficient Fund" vide cheque return memo dated 21.08.2017.

Complaint u/sec.
138/141/142 of the Negotiable Instrument Act, 1881 was filed by plaintiff against the defendant firm and its partners which is still pending.

7. Drawing conclusion from the conduct of the defendant it has been claimed defendant had a malafide intention of cheating and defrauding the plaintiff as neither the plaintiff was made a partner nor the amount invested by her was returned/paid back.

Hence this suit for recovery of Rs.
28,04,000/- which includes the principal amount of Rs. 23,00,000/- and interest @ 12% per annum from 21.08.2017 till filing of the suit.
8. Summons of the suit were sent to the defendant firm and the same were duly served upon it.

When initially suit was instituted on 16/17.10.2019 there was only one defendant i.e. the partnership firm namely M/s AAA Hospitality but later on one application u/O VI R 17 CPC was filed by plaintiff on 19.12.2022 for impleading the past and current partners of the firm in array of defendants which was allowed vide order dated 13.03.2023 and defendant No. 2 to 9 were impleaded besides the original defendant firm (now defendant No. 1).
9. Summons sent to defendant No. 5 returned back with report that Mr. Ashutosh Kanodia had expired in 2019.
Hence, subsequently, name of defendant No. 5 was deleted from array of parties vide order dated 27.04.2023 on the statement of Ld. Counsel for plaintiff that he did not want to implead his LRs.

10. The defendant No. 1 firm in its written statement filed under the signature of defendant No.3 has taken certain preliminary objections and denied the case of the plaintiff on merits.
It is stated that the plaintiff has concealed the material facts and the suit is without cause of action.
It is stated that neither the cheque in question was issued by the partners of the defendant firm nor the firm owes any contractual or other liability towards the plaintiff.

It is claimed that the present partnership firm namely M/s AAA Hospitality is a reconstituted partnership firm and the erstwhile partners who had the dealings with the plaintiff are no more partners in the present firm.

It is pleaded that the plaintiff has not joined/arrayed the erstwhile partnership firm named M/s AAA Hospitality having its principal place of business/registered office at A-58, Third Floor, Ashok Vihar, Phase-I, Delhi-52 nor the partners of the said firm have been made party.

It is stated that there is no privity of contract between the plaintiff and the defendant firm or its partners as all dealings have taken place between the plaintiff and erstwhile partnership firm and its partners.

11. Defendant No. 2 Mr. Yogesh Verma, in his separate written statement claimed that the suit is not maintainable against him as he had joined the partnership firm on 31.03.2019 as investor/sleeping partner.

Further, that it was agreed among the retiring/continuing and new partners of the defendant No. 1 firm that the defendant No. 2 would not be an active partner and would not be liable for any business liabilities, tax demands, litigation, penalties, dues etc. before the date of his joining the reconstituted firm.

Further pleaded that Mr. Pradeep Goel having 35% share and Mr.
Manoj Kumar having 50% share were responsible for all such liabilities.
12. Defendant No. 3 and 4 adopted the Written Statement of Defendant No.1 vide statement of their counsel recorded on 04.07.2023.
13. The defendant No. 6 Mr. Pankaj Gupta filed a separate written statement in which several preliminary objections have been taken including the objection pertaining to bar of limitation.
On merits, it is submitted that husband of the plaintiff had approached the defendant for investment of funds in the business as he was friend of the partners of the defendant firm.

It is admitted that husband of the plaintiff was assured that her name would be included in the partnership business and her involvement with the defendant firm would bring greater returns and higher profits subject to investment of Rs. 33,00,000/-.

It is contended that despite the assurance, the husband of the plaintiff decided not to be part of the business rather he was more interested in getting handsome return out of the investment and decided not to join the partnership as in case of her joining the partnership the plaintiff would have to share loss if any of the partnership business.
Other averments made in the plaint are denied.

14. Defendant No. 7 Mr. Kunal Babuta filed his separate written statement and claimed that suit was not maintainable against him as he had retired from the firm on 31.03.2019 and it was agreed that the new partners and the retiring partners would not be responsible for any business liabilities.

sentences.text: He contended that none of the past and current partners brought on record the books of account of the firm of the relevant period and he thus called for drawing of an adverse inference against them as books of account would have shown amount standing to the credit of the plaintiff and still unpaid to plaintiff.

He further contended that none of the documents exhibited by the defendants could be said to have been proved as original thereof were never brought to the court or on record and thus they were inadmissible.

He further contended that it was admitted by almost all the defendants that they neither gave public notice of retirement nor of inclusion, hence they all were liable to plaintiff being partner past and present.
He further contended interse dispute about partners and proposed partner qua the business transaction qualifies as a commercial dispute.

He further contended that plaintiff last legs of her fund was infused in August, 2016, she received Rs. 10 lacs in April 2017 and the cheque in question was given in July, 2017 while the present suit was filed on 16/17.10.2017 and thus the suit was well within limitation.
31. Taking this Court to case of the plaintiff and testimony in cross examination of PW1 and also documents admitted by the PW1 in his cross examination, cumulative argument of Ld.

Counsels for defendants could be summarized to the effect that plaintiff had concealed material facts as plaintiff was required to place the truth as subsequently admitted by PW1 in his cross examination and plaintiff by concealing the same from the court not only attempted to play fraud upon the court but also upon the defendants.
The suit was not maintainable against the subsequently added all the partners as no pre-litigation mediation was undertaken with those subsequently added defendants.
Plaintiff deliberately did not implead the partners of the firm despite being insiders of the firm as she wanted to have favourable order in their absence.

PW1/husband/attorney of the plaintiff was there in the firm as late as in 2018 and if at all the then partner's of the firm were allegedly fooling the plaintiff why her husband/attorney was managing the affairs of the firm even after the alleged dishonour of the cheque which fact show that PW1 misused the cheque.
The retiring partner and the new partners were not liable for the liability, if any, of the firm, in view of terms of various partnership deed retiring old partners and including new partners.
Plaintiff's infusion of fund was her share of capital or that of her husband and they always remained there in firm actively.
Objection qua the absence of original documents relied upon by the defendants was not sustainable in law as PW1 admitted there execution and participation.
Hence, they sought dismissal of the suit.

sentences.text: 34. As noted above by way of application under Order VI Rule 17 CPC plaintiff impleaded the then partners of defendant No.1 and subsisting/new partners of the firm.

Plaintiff, who filed the present suit through her husband as an attorney claiming that even otherwise he was personally aware of the facts of the case, did not disclose the name of past or subsisting partners at the time of filling of the suit.
Even names of those partners who were there at the time of alleged taking money from the plaintiff or who kept on avoiding inclusion of the plaintiff into partnership was not mentioned.

It is interesting note that despite impleadment of past and subsisting/new partners, plaintiff did not make necessary amendment in the plaint so as to specify roles allegedly played by the then partners relevant for the plaintiff's case.

Moreover, impleadment of partners were done on the basis of information provided by the firm which filed its Written Statement through Manoj Tushir (who was subsequently impleaded as defendant No.3) and thus thereby plaintiff again conveyed the feeling that plaintiff and for that matter her husband was not aware of the then partners, if not the subsisting partners, even though plaintiff had filed complaint under Section 138 of NI Act against some of the then partners.

Conduct of the plaintiff in concealing the name of at least the then partners (or at least of those partners against whom she had filed complaint under N.I. Act) could not be for any reason other than malafide intention.

ISSUE No. 6:- Whether the suit is not maintainable against defendant No. 6, 7, 8 & 9?

OPD. 
56
. Onus to prove this issue is upon the defendants.

It was admitted by PW1 that plaintiff had dropped defendant No.6 from the complaint under Section 138 N.I Act which was filed for dishounour of the cheque dt. 15.07.2017 Mark-E for Rs. 23 lacs allegedly given by the defendant firm.
Partnership firm is not a legal entity and it always acts through its partners.
If partnership firm had issued cheque for discharge of its liability and is sued, all of its partners would be liable jointly and severely.
If plaintiff has discharged one of the partners it would have the effect of discharging the firm and its other partners.
Hence, after discharging defendant No.6 from the alleged liability under the cheque issued for and on behalf of the firm, the liability of other partners also stood discharged.
However it is not clear from the evidence whether the discharge of defendant No.6 took place before filling of the present suit or after the present suit.

If discharge had taken place during the pendency of the present suit, then suit is maintainable against the defendant as the relevant for above issue would be date of filing but if the discharge had taken place prior to institution of the suit then suit would not be maintainable against the firm as well as its partner.
Hence, Issue No.6 is decided accordingly.

sentences.text: 59. In Kailash Devi Khanna v. DD Global Capital Ltd. 2019 SCC Online Del 9954 Hon'ble Delhi High Court emphasized that not all suits for monetary recovery qualify as "commercial dispute" under the Act of 2015.

entities.text: Kailash Devi Khanna v. DD Global Capital Ltd. 2019 SCC Online Del 9954
entities.label: PRECEDENT

sentences.text:
The Court specifically observed that for a claim to fall under Section 2(1)(c)(i) of the Act of 2015, it must pertain to "ordinary transactions of merchants, bankers, financiers, and traders,"
involving mercantile documents and their enforcement or interpretation.

The Court further held that a suit merely seeking recovery of money, without any connection to mercantile transactions or documents, does not meet the criteria of a "commercial dispute" and, therefore, cannot be filed as a commercial suit.

Filing a civil suit under the commercial courts' jurisdiction, without meeting these requirements, amounts to a misuse of the specialized forum meant for expeditious resolution of genuine business disputes, ultimately hindering the adjudication of legitimate commercial cases.
60. Interse dispute between the merchants, banker, financier and traders qua transaction connected with their business do qualify as "commercial dispute".
Accordingly, issue No.8 is decided against the defendant No.8 and in favour of plaintiff.

opennyai_summary.ANALYSIS:
Conduct of the plaintiff in concealing the name of at least the then partners (or at least of those partners against whom she had filed complaint under N.I. Act) could not be for any reason other than malafide intention.
He Sakshi Mittal vs M/S Aaa Hospitality on 20 December, 2025 Indian Kanoon - http://indiankanoon.org/doc/36322813/
9 admitted that plaintiff had voluntarily dropped the name of defendant No.6 from the complaint under Section 138 of N.I. Act.
The case of the defendant was to the effect that he became partner in defendant No.1 vide deed of 01.04.2019 Ex D8W1/5 and it had condition/clause to the effect that new partners would not be responsible for any business liabilities and thus, defendant No,2 pleads that suit against him was not maintainable.
Plaintiff could not cross examine D2W1 (defendant No.1) to dispute that he became partner only on 01.04.2019.
Yet assuming that plaintiff had been held entitle to her claim against the firm then defendant would have been liable as partner, even though he in his turn would be entitled to recover the same from partnership firm or from other partners in accordance with their share, due to the clause making him not responsible for firm's previous liability.
Under Indian Partnership Act, 1932,
liability of past, present and future partners depends upon public notice to third party and/or agreement with the third party.
Thus, this issue would have been decided against the defendant if plaintiff had been held entitle to her claim in the present suit.
Purely speaking on the basis of the stand of the defendants that since plaintiff was partner and was always there through her husband, hence she was not entitled to refund of her investment and therefore, plaintiff had no cause of action.
Consequently issue of limitation does not arise.
Thus, present suit cannot be said to barred by limitation.
Partnership firm is not a legal entity and it always acts through its partners.
If partnership firm had issued cheque for discharge of its liability and is sued, all of its partners would be liable jointly and severely.
If plaintiff has discharged one of the partners it would have the effect of discharging the firm and its other partners.
Hence, after discharging defendant No.6 from the alleged liability under the cheque issued for and on behalf of the firm, the liability of other partners also stood discharged.
However it is not clear from the evidence whether the discharge of defendant No.6 took place before filling of the present suit or after the present suit.
Plaintiff had initiated mandatory pre-litigation mediation which failed as per report dt. 01.10.2019.
Plaintiff has properly verified the suit and has also filed statement of truth by way of affidavit.
Defendant No. 2 to 9 were impleaded as past and present partner of defendant No.1 and not in their personal capacity and admittedly defendant No.1 was served for pre- litigation mediation which necessarily implies mediation with partners.
Therefore, there is no non-compliance of Section 12A of CC Act.
Hence, issue No. 7 is decided against the defendants No. 6 & 8 and in favour of plaintiff.
As per plaintiff she infused the funds in the partnership firm to become partner to make profit (and suffer loss too) out of the commercial transaction of the firm.
As per defendants she was partner except for name and her husband was looking after the day to day affairs of the firm as partner for the funds Sakshi Mittal vs M/S Aaa Hospitality on 20 December, 2025 Indian Kanoon - http://indiankanoon.org/doc/36322813/
15 infused by her.
59. In Kailash Devi Khanna v. DD Global Capital Ltd. 2019 SCC Online Del 9954 Hon'ble Delhi High Court emphasized that not all suits for monetary recovery qualify as "commercial dispute" under the Act of 2015.
The Court further held that a suit merely seeking recovery of money, without any connection to mercantile transactions or documents, does not meet the criteria of a "commercial dispute" and, therefore, cannot be filed as a commercial suit.
Filing a civil suit under the commercial courts' jurisdiction, without meeting these requirements, amounts to a misuse of the specialized forum meant for expeditious resolution of genuine business disputes, ultimately hindering the adjudication of legitimate commercial cases.
